title_en: Fragments on the Letter to the Galatians
author: Gennadius of Constantinople
occasion: Fragmentary exegetical remarks on Paul's Letter to the Galatians, explaining how the Mosaic law served as a temporary guardian until the coming of Christ, who alone mediates for all nations.
argument: Gennadius argues that Moses mediated the law to only one nation, whereas Christ, being both truly God and truly human, mediates for all nations and unites them in himself. The law was not given to nullify the blessings but served as a protective wall restraining sin until the justification by faith was revealed. The 'elements of the world' are interpreted not as sun and moon, which Gennadius thinks Paul would not have meant because subjection to them would be unprofitable, but as the introductory law given to the Jews, or alternatively as observances concerning days, water, and fire. He also warns that certain teachers feign acceptance of the Galatians' faith in Christ only to draw them away after themselves.

outline.move: Contrasts Moses' mediation for one nation with Christ's universal mediation as both God and man.
Explains that the law was not given to destroy the blessings but to restrain sin until justification by faith.
Interprets the 'elements of the world' as the introductory law for the immature, rejecting sun and moon as unprofitable objects of subjection.
Offers an alternative reading of the elements as observances of days, water, and fire.
Warns that certain teachers feign acceptance of the Galatians' faith in Christ only to draw them away after themselves.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul is quoted or paraphrased with phrases like Λέγει τοίνυν ὅτι and φησίν in sections u01-open, u01-rem-early, u01-rem-close
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Λέγει τοίνυν ὅτι Μωϋσῆς μὲν ἐμεσίτευσε...
_unresolved_facts.fix: In u01-open, Λέγει τοίνυν ὅτι introduces Gennadius's own summary of Paul's argument about Moses and Christ, not a direct quotation of Paul. In u01-rem-early and u01-rem-close, φησίν refers to Paul (the implied subject of the commentary). However, the marking 'Λέγει τοίνυν ὅτι' in u01-open introduces Gennadius's own interpretive statement, not a Pauline quotation per se.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Eusebius: 'Mentioned as having said something strange on this topic in the fourth book of his Proof of the Gospel.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὅρα δὲ τί εἶπεν εἰς τοῦτο ξένον ὁ Εὐσέβιος ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ λόγῳ τῆς Εὐαγγελικῆς ἀποδείξεως
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eusebius is mentioned as having said something 'ξένον' (strange/novel) on this topic. However, the brief should note that Gennadius is directing the reader to look at what Eusebius said—he does not quote or summarize Eusebius's actual view, only flags it as worth examining.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-close contains two moves: 'Offers an alternative reading of the elements as observances of days, water, and fire' and 'Warns that certain teachers feign acceptance of the Galatians' faith in Christ only to draw them away after themselves'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline should indicate that u01-rem-close contains three distinct moves: (1) the alternative reading of elements as observances (days, water, fire), (2) the reference to Eusebius's strange statement, and (3) the warning about teachers feigning acceptance of faith. The Eusebius reference is a separate move that is currently omitted from the outline.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Gennadius argues that Moses mediated the law to only one nation, whereas Christ... mediates for all nations
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Λέγει τοίνυν ὅτι Μωϋσῆς μὲν ἐμεσίτευσε πρὸς τὴν δόσιν τοῦ νόμου, ἀλλ' ἑνὶ μόνον ἐμεσίτευσεν ἔθνει
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says Μωϋσῆς mediated πρὸς τὴν δόσιν τοῦ νόμου (toward the giving of the law), not 'the law' simpliciter. More importantly, Λέγει τοίνυν ὅτι indicates this is Paul's argument (or Gennadius's reading of Paul's argument), not necessarily Gennadius's own independent argument. The brief should distinguish between reported argument and authorial claim.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The 'elements of the world' are interpreted not as sun and moon, which Gennadius thinks Paul would not have meant because subjection to them would be unprofitable
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὐκ ἄν, ὡς οἶμαι, ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην ἔλαβεν εἰς τάξιν τῶν ἐπιτρόπων διὰ τὸ ἀσύμφορον εἶναι τὴν εἰς ταῦτα ὑποταγήν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Gennadius says 'οὐκ ἄν, ὡς οἶμαι' (he would not, as I think)—the ὡς οἶμαι marks this as Gennadius's own opinion about what Paul would have meant, not what Paul actually said. The reason given is that subjection to them would be ἀσύμφορον (unprofitable/inexpedient), not that Paul 'would not have meant' it. The brief should preserve the modal/hedged nature of Gennadius's claim.
